name: Deoxyarbutin
lead: Deoxyarbutin (dA) is a synthetic derivative of arbutin that inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme that drives melanin production, and has been developed as a topical skin-lightening agent for hyperpigmentation such as age spots and melasma [1][4].

It was described in a 2005 paper as a reversible tyrosinase inhibitor with skin-lightening activity in a pigmented guinea pig model and with inhibition of mushroom tyrosinase more potent than hydroquinone or arbutin in vitro [1]. Later laboratory work has examined its safety relative to hydroquinone, and its stability in formulations [2][8]. The sources reviewed contain no randomized human trial results for deoxyarbutin as a cosmetic.

paras: Tyrosinase inhibitors of this type resemble the enzyme's substrate, tyrosine, and compete for the catalytic site; deoxyarbutin was designed on this premise [1]. A 2008 study reported on the mechanism of inhibition by deoxyarbutin and its second-generation derivatives [4]. Another study found that deoxyarbutin and derivatives reduced tyrosinase activity and melanin synthesis without inducing reactive oxygen species or apoptosis in the cells tested [9].

A 2022 comparison of tyrosinase inhibitors noted that reported results for kojic acid, arbutins and deoxyarbutin differ between articles, and examined these compounds against mushroom tyrosinase and cultured B16F10 cells [3].

The safety of hydroquinone and its derivatives as whitening agents has been described as controversial, and a 2009 study compared hydroquinone, arbutin and deoxyarbutin in cultured melanocytes with and without UVA-induced oxidative stress to assess whether deoxyarbutin could be an alternative [2]. A 2017 study examined hydroquinone-mediated cytotoxicity and hypopigmentation effects from UVB-irradiated arbutin and deoxyarbutin [6]. Stability of deoxyarbutin in an anhydrous emulsion has also been studied [8]. A 2006 paper reported a comparative efficacy and safety evaluation [5].

A 2022 animal study investigated deoxyarbutin in severe acute pancreatitis, unrelated to appearance [7]. A 2020 article discusses deoxyarbutin as a hydroquinone alternative for topical skin lightening [10].
No studies found of randomized human trials in the sources reviewed; the evidence consists of in vitro work, an animal (guinea pig) study, and formulation and safety studies [1][2][5].

card.summary: A synthetic arbutin derivative that blocks tyrosinase in lab and animal work; human trial data are thin.
card.note: Evidence is mostly in vitro and animal; one study examined UVB-irradiated deoxyarbutin cytotoxicity.

quick.overview:
Deoxyarbutin is a lab-made relative of arbutin studied as a skin-lightening ingredient for dark spots and uneven pigment.

It was reported in 2005 to lighten skin in guinea pigs and to inhibit tyrosinase more potently than hydroquinone in a test-tube assay. Published human trials were not found in the sources reviewed.
quick.mechanism: It competes with tyrosine at tyrosinase, the enzyme that makes melanin, reducing melanin production; studies describe the inhibition as reversible.
quick.risks: Researchers have compared its safety with hydroquinone in cultured cells and examined cytotoxicity of UVB-irradiated forms. Regulatory status was not established in the sources reviewed.
